title: Even Mild Sleep Deprivation May Lead to Weight Gain
gist: A Columbia University trial of 95 at-risk adults found that delaying bedtime by 90 minutes for six weeks — cutting sleep by about 80 minutes, the mild deficit affecting roughly 30 percent of adults — raised average weight by about 0.45 kg and increased daily sedentary time by 17 minutes (nearly 30 for men and postmenopausal women). Leptin rose rather than fell, contradicting the hormone-disruption overeating theory from severe-restriction studies; companion analyses of the same cohort found higher insulin resistance and more inflammation-seeking immune cells.

insights.claim: A Columbia University trial of 95 adults who normally slept at least seven hours and carried cardiovascular and metabolic risk delayed bedtimes by 90 minutes for six weeks, cutting sleep by about 80 minutes and raising average weight by roughly 0.45 kilogram versus their normal-sleep period.
insights.speaker: Ritsuko Kawai
insights.so_what: A pound of gain in six weeks from a routine sleep deficit extrapolates to clinically meaningful annual weight gain across a very large population.
